title: Tartarus
hook: Does Peter's one mention of Tartarus prove humans will burn in hell forever?
tldr: No. In 2 Peter 2:4 Tartarus is a borrowed cultural image for the dark place where rebellious angels await judgment. Its chains of darkness are likely symbolic, and whether read literally or symbolically, it concerns angels, never humans, so it cannot be equated with hellfire.
big_idea: Tartarus holds rebellious angels for judgment; it is not hellfire for humans.

points.title: Used only once in the New Testament
points.text: Tartarus appears only in 2 Peter 2:4, where God casts sinning angels into it and commits them to pits of darkness, held for judgment.

points.title: A borrowed cultural image
points.text: In Greek myth Tartarus was a dungeon for the defeated Titans. Peter uses the familiar concept to make a point, without endorsing the mythology, as Christians today use cultural references.

points.title: Known in Jewish literature
points.text: Tartarus appears in the Septuagint of Job and in the Greek Book of Enoch, where the archangel Uriel is in charge of it as the prison of 200 fallen angels.

points.title: Chains of darkness are symbolic
points.text: If all sinful angels were bound, how could Jesus meet evil spirits and Satan still prowl? The chains likely picture fear of coming judgment, as Wisdom of Solomon calls Egypt's darkness a chain.

points.title: No humans in Tartarus
points.text: Even read literally, Peter never says humans are sent to Tartarus, and Scripture never teaches that humans suffer there. It cannot be a place of eternal torment for people.

sections.summary: 2 Peter 2:4-6 is ambiguous and much debated, and supporters of eternal conscious torment often cite it for hellfire. But context and intertextual allusions point elsewhere. The passage says God did not spare sinning angels but cast them into tartaroō and pits of darkness, held for judgment; did not spare the ancient world but protected Noah and seven others; and reduced Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes as an example for the ungodly.

sections.h: Tartarus as metaphor in Jewish texts
sections.summary: Tartarus is used metaphorically for the gloomy, dark place where rebellious angels are held awaiting judgment. It appears in the Septuagint translation of Job 40:20 and 41:24 and in Hellenistic Jewish literature such as the Greek Book of Enoch, where God puts the archangel Uriel 'in charge of the world and of Tartarus' (Enoch 20:2), understood as the prison of 200 fallen angels.

Tartarus appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:4, where God casts sinning angels into it and delivers them in chains of darkness awaiting judgment. To understand Peter, we must identify both the symbolism of Tartarus and the event he refers to.

In Greek mythology Tartarus is both a primordial deity and a place: a dungeon for the Titans, the second generation of primordial deities defeated by the Olympians. Some humans, such as King Sisyphus and King Tantalus, were said to be sent there for severe crimes. Peter does not endorse the myth; like Christians using cultural references today, he borrows a familiar idea to show the severe consequences of the angels' rebellion.

Peter's bound angels could point to two events. Some see the angelic rebellion of Isaiah 14:12-21 and Ezekiel 28:1-19. Others see Genesis 6:1-4, where the sons of God fathered the Nephilim with the daughters of men, supported by 1 Peter 3:19-20 and Jude 6 on spirits in prison and angels bound in Noah's days, whom Peter also mentions. Both face a problem: if all were bound, how did Jesus meet evil spirits, and how is Satan active (1 Peter 5:8)?

If symbolic, the chains may be the fear and anticipation of judgment that immobilize the rebellious angels. Wisdom of Solomon 17:17 calls the ninth plague of darkness in Egypt a 'chain of darkness', symbolically. The angels are constrained by knowledge of coming judgment, not physical chains, fitting the biblical theme of judgment bringing chaos back into submission. Even read literally, no humans are sent to Tartarus, so it cannot equal hellfire for humans.

2 Peter 2:4-6 does not teach hellfire or eternal conscious torment. The dark abyss symbolizes chaos and disorder, not eternal suffering. Literal or symbolic, Tartarus concerns the judgment of rebellious angels, not humans. Context, intertextual allusions and symbolic language show Peter stressing the severe consequences of rebellion against God, in line with the biblical story of judgment and the ultimate restoration of order in creation.

yes.label: Literal prison
yes.note: Still only angels are there. Scripture never sends humans to Tartarus, so it is not human hellfire.

no.note: Fear of coming judgment immobilizes the angels, like Egypt's 'chain of darkness' in Wisdom of Solomon 17:17.

quiz.q: How many times does Tartarus appear in the New Testament?
quiz.why: Only in 2 Peter 2:4, about sinning angels held for judgment.

quiz.q: Who does Peter say is sent to Tartarus?
quiz.why: Peter speaks of rebellious angels; Scripture never teaches that humans suffer in Tartarus.

quiz.q: Which text calls Egypt's plague of darkness a 'chain of darkness'?
quiz.why: Wisdom of Solomon uses the phrase symbolically, supporting a symbolic reading of Peter's chains.

reflect: Why might a single borrowed word like Tartarus have been made to carry so much weight in debates about hell?
